tongan_seketoa.name: manifests in the sea as a great shark heralded by two remora
tongan_seketoa.notes: When the Maatu chief of Niuatoputapu wishes to consult him, kava root is cast into the sea; two remora (his matapule attendants) come first, then Seketoa appears as a large shark.

sources.reference: E. E. V. Collocott, 'Notes on Tongan Religion', Journal of the Polynesian Society (1921)

tongan_seketoa.name: guards and answers the chiefs and people of Niuatoputapu and Tafahi
tongan_seketoa.notes: As deified ancestor of the Maatu line he serves as the tutelary protector of his island, giving counsel and aid to his descendants.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Seketoa'

topiltzin.name: performs autosacrificial blood-penance as model priest
topiltzin.notes: The Anales de Cuauhtitlan present Topiltzin Ce Acatl Quetzalcoatl as the holy priest-king who drew his own blood in penance and instituted Toltec religious observance at Tollan.

sources.reference: Anales de Cuauhtitlan (Codex Chimalpopoca)

toraja_puang_matua.name: forges the first ancestors of humans, creatures and crops in his sky-smithy
toraja_puang_matua.notes: In Aluk To Dolo myth Puang Matua creates Datu Laukku' (the female ancestor), cotton, cattle, plants and the rest from pure gold by means of the bellows Sauan Sibarrung in his house above the middle of the sky.

sources.reference: Hetty Nooy-Palm, The Sa'dan-Toraja: A Study of Their Social Life and Religion (1979)

toraja_puang_matua.name: hands down the ritual law (aluk) and customs to the first humans
toraja_puang_matua.notes: Puang Matua transmits the Aluk To Dolo, the body of ritual prescription, to Datu Laukku' and her line; the houses of men imitate his sky-house.

sources.reference: Hetty Nooy-Palm, The Sa'dan-Toraja: A Study of Their Social Life and Religion (1979)

totonac_aktsini.name: strikes the clouds with his axe to make thunder and lightning
totonac_aktsini.notes: Aktsini' (Trueno Viejo) wields a hammer or axe that produces thunder and lightning as it strikes the clouds, and pours rain-water from his other hand.

sources.reference: Alain Ichon, La religion des Totonaques de la Sierra (1969)

totonac_aktsini.name: heads the Twelve Old Thunderbolts who dwell in the ruins of El Tajin
totonac_aktsini.notes: As Thunder Lord he commands the collective storm-beings (Tajin) believed to inhabit the ancient city named for him.

sources.reference: Isabel Kelly & Angel Palerm, The Tajin Totonac (1952)

tuamotuan_faumea.name: holds the wind in the sweat of her armpit and releases it to speed canoes
tuamotuan_faumea.notes: In the rescue of Hina-arau-riki from the octopus-demon Rogo-tumu-here, Faumea releases the wind held in her armpit at Takaroa's command to drive the canoe.

sources.reference: Martha Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (1940), Tuamotuan parallels

tuamotuan_hina.name: pilots and names the islands from the bow of the voyaging canoe
tuamotuan_hina.notes: As Hina-fa'auru-va'a she stands at the bow of Ru's canoe Te-apori, naming the lands they sight while Ru raises the sky and steers the circumnavigation.

sources.reference: Kenneth P. Emory, Tuamotuan Religious Structures and Ceremonies (1947)

tuamotuan_hina.name: watches over night travellers from the moon
tuamotuan_hina.notes: Having stepped into the moon (Hina-i-aa-i-te-marama), she watches over voyagers by night, an office that earned her the byname Great Hina the watchwoman.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928)

tuamotuan_ru.name: circumnavigates the ocean in his canoe Te-apori, fixing the world's quarters
tuamotuan_ru.notes: Ru ('the Transplanter') sets the bounds of the world, naming east Te-hitia-o-te-ra and west Te-too-a-o-te-ra, voyaging with his sister Hina at the bow.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928)

tsimshian_chief_of_heaven.name: keeps the daylight, sun, moon and stars in the box Maa in his sky-house
tsimshian_chief_of_heaven.notes: While the earth lay in dusk, the Chief of Heaven hoarded the light in the box called Maa; the Raven, reborn as his grandson, cries for it and carries it off.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology (1916)

tsimshian_logobola.name: holds back the fresh water and rules the fog
tsimshian_logobola.notes: Logobola ('the Lazy One'), brother and rival of Txamsem, withholds the clear water and is bound up with the fog into which the Raven strays; their contest fixes the world's waters.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology (1916)

tupi_maira.name: looses a destroying flood upon mankind
tupi_maira.notes: In the version reported by Thevet (1550s), Maire (Maira-Monan) sets out to destroy the world by a great flood, a counterpart to Monan's destruction by fire.

sources.reference: Andre Thevet, Les Singularitez de la France Antarctique (1557)

turkic_asena.name: bears the wounded child across the sea to the cave of refuge
turkic_asena.notes: Carrying the sole maimed survivor, the she-wolf crosses the Western Sea to a cave by the Qocho mountains, where she bears the ten founding sons.

sources.reference: Zhoushu (Book of Zhou), 'Account of the Tujue'
Bernardino de Sahagun, Florentine Codex, Book 3

tongan_seketoa.name: kava-summoning of Seketoa by the Maatu chiefs of Niuatoputapu
tongan_seketoa.cadence: as needed (when the chief seeks counsel)
tongan_seketoa.notes: The Maatu chief sends his matapule to cast kava root into the sea; the two remora come, then Seketoa appears as a shark to answer. A continuous local tutelary cult of the deified shark-ancestor.

sources.reference: E. E. V. Collocott, 'Notes on Tongan Religion', Journal of the Polynesian Society (1921)

totonac_aktsini.name: rain-and-thunder observances directed to Trueno Viejo at El Tajin
totonac_aktsini.notes: The Totonac of the Sierra honour Aktsini'/Trueno Viejo as bringer of the storms; the ruined city of El Tajin, named for the thunder, is regarded as the dwelling of him and the Twelve Thunderbolts.

sources.reference: Alain Ichon, La religion des Totonaques de la Sierra (1969)

turkic_erlik.name: black-animal sacrifice to Erlik by the black shamans (kara kam)
turkic_erlik.notes: Where white animals were offered upward to Ulgen, black animals were offered to the underworld lord Erlik; the kara kam who treated with him conducted these rites.

sources.reference: Uno Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology (1927)

attributes.name: the wind-jewel (ehecacozcatl), a conch-shell cross-section worn as a pectoral
attributes.notes: The spiral wind-jewel marks his identification with Quetzalcoatl in his Ehecatl (wind) aspect.

sources.reference: Bernardino de Sahagun, Florentine Codex, Book 3

attributes.name: rings over the eyes like spectacles, with a headdress
attributes.notes: Aktzin is typically shown as a male figure with goggle-like rings around the eyes, holding an axe/hammer in one hand and pouring water from the other.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Aktzin'

sacredPlants.name: maize (the corn she brings forth and embodies)

sources.reference: Alain Ichon, La religion des Totonaques de la Sierra (1969)

sacredAnimals.name: the raven, the form he wears as transformer

sources.reference: Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology (1916)

sacredAnimals.name: the shark, the form Puna takes as sovereign of Hiti-marama

sources.reference: J. Frank Stimson, Tuamotuan Legends (1937)

sacredAnimals.name: the moon, which she enters and inhabits
sacredAnimals.notes: Not an animal but her defining celestial seat; recorded as her abiding emblem.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928)

sacredAnimals.name: the grey/blue she-wolf herself, totem and banner-emblem of the Ashina
sacredAnimals.notes: The wolf-head appeared on Gokturk standards as a totem of martial prowess and heavenly mandate.

sources.reference: Zhoushu (Book of Zhou), 'Account of the Tujue'

attributes.name: lord of darkness and the nine layers of the lower world
attributes.notes: Imagined as the black, subterranean counterpart to the bright sky-god Ulgen, ruling the ninth depth of the earth.

sources.reference: Uno Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology (1927)

sacredAnimals.name: the plover, the bird-form in which Tangaloa descends to 'Ata to make the first men

sources.reference: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924)

attributes.name: the toa (casuarina/ironwood) tree reaching to the sky, by which he descends
attributes.notes: A great toa growing on Toonangakava is the ladder by which Tangaloa 'Eitumatupu'a climbs down to earth and his son 'Aho'eitu climbs up to the sky.

sources.reference: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924)

attributes.name: the sun itself, source of light and warmth
attributes.notes: Guaraci (Tupi kuarahy) is the personified Sun, twin to the Moon Jaci; with Jaci he is pursued across the sky by the great blue jaguar that causes eclipses.

sources.reference: Alfred Metraux, La religion des Tupinamba (1928)

attributes.name: the moon itself, guardian of the night
attributes.notes: Jaci (Tupi jasy) is the personified Moon, protector of night, lovers and reproduction; in Tupinamba myth menaced by the jaguar identified with the planet Mars.

sources.reference: Alfred Metraux, La religion des Tupinamba (1928)

sacredAnimals.name: the jaguar, slayer of their mother and quarry of their vengeance

sources.reference: Alfred Metraux, La religion des Tupinamba (1928)

sacredPlants.name: the yam, which he gave to the people in place of human flesh
sacredPlants.notes: As culture-hero Tudava ends cannibalism by teaching the cultivation of yams (and taro), the staple of Trobriand life.

sources.reference: Bronislaw Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922)

attributes.name: the first ancestor wrought from pure gold by Puang Matua
attributes.notes: Datu Laukku' is made directly by the creator from pure gold in the sky-smithy, the progenitor from whom the Toraja descend.

sources.reference: Hetty Nooy-Palm, The Sa'dan-Toraja: A Study of Their Social Life and Religion (1979)

sacredAnimals.name: the fish and creatures of the deep, his dominion as lord of the sea

sources.reference: Kenneth P. Emory, 'Tuamotuan Concepts of Creation', Journal of the Polynesian Society (1940)
